query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloys produced via spark plasma sintering, samples sintered at a lower temperature (1300 °C) that yield a fine-grained BCC matrix with a higher fraction of finely dispersed Laves phases will exhibit approximately 40% lower wear mass loss and 30% reduced corrosion rate in H2SO4 compared to samples sintered at a higher temperature (1400 °C) which have coarser microstructures.
generation.material_initial_state: CrMoNbWV HEA produced by mechanical alloying, consolidated by spark plasma sintering with initial fine-grained BCC structure.
generation.intervention: Control the sintering temperature: compare samples sintered at 1300 °C versus those sintered at 1400 °C.
generation.conditions: Electrochemical corrosion tests in H2SO4 solution and wear tests under consistent mechanical loading at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: A fine-grained BCC matrix reinforced by finely dispersed Laves phase precipitates which collectively provide high hardness and reduced defect propagation.
generation.mechanism: Lower sintering temperatures promote grain refinement and optimal dispersion of secondary phases, which collectively enhance both the mechanical barrier to wear and the integrity of the passive film against corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: The 1300 °C-sintered sample will show ≈40% lower wear mass loss and ≈30% lower corrosion rate compared to the 1400 °C-sintered sample, under otherwise matched conditions.
generation.baseline: CrMoNbWV HEA samples sintered at 1400 °C with coarser microstructure and lower fraction of reinforcing Laves phases.
generation.boundary: The mechanism should be effective provided processing-induced defects are minimized; if porosity or oxide inclusions dominate the microstructure, the benefits may not be realized.
generation.uncertainty: Variability in SPS consolidation parameters and slight compositional inhomogeneities may affect the quantitative differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of CrMoNbWV HEA samples by SPS at 1300 °C and 1400 °C, ensuring similar densities. Perform standardized wear tests (using Archard’s approach) and electrochemical corrosion measurements in H2SO4 on both sets.
measurements: Grain size and phase distribution (via SEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 1300 °C-sintered samples do not exhibit the predicted (~40% lower wear and ~30% lower corrosion rate) improvements relative to the 1400 °C samples, or if microstructural characterization shows no significant differences in grain refinement and phase dispersion, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Simultaneously, the presence of the fine-grained Laves phases protects the surface from strong plastic deformations and prevents destructions during a sliding, while the BCC solid solution of high plasticity protects the surface from a brittle fracture. The increase of the SPS temperature results in a decrease of the Laves phase content in the samples. The Laves phase grains coarsen, leading to higher wear under the tests. The higher characteristics of the carburized layer probably result from the BCC-lattice strain caused by the intercalation of carbon atoms and the fine-dispersed HEA carbides. The difference in the wear rate for the carburized layer and the bulk HEA corresponds to the Archard wear equation. According to the equation, sliding wear resistance is proportional to the alloy hardness. The difference between the values for the carburized layer and the bulk HEA is 300%, indicating the superior wear resistance of the carburized layer compared to the conventional hard alloys. The bulk HEA exhibits wear resistance higher than a sintered SiC, or SiC/B4C composite does.

Refractory CrMoNbWV HEA was obtained from elemental powders by mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering.The phase composition, microstructure, and properties of the manufactured alloy depended strongly on the sintering conditions. It was determined that in the MA-powder with a BCC solid solution structure, the Laves phases Cr2Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb precipitate under the SPS (41.6 vol.% at 1200 °C). Their volume fraction decreases when the SPS temperature increases and accounts for 21.5 vol.% at 1300 °C and 11.5 vol.% at 1400 °C. The presence of the oxides NbVO4–VO can be connected with the powder oxidation during the MA.The sintered samples exhibit the compressive strength of 2700–2870 MPa. The samples’ low plasticity is caused by the high volume fraction of the Laves phases localized at the grain boundaries. In the sample sintered at 1400 °C, the volume fraction of the Laves phases is lowered. However, the particle size of the oxides increases significantly. The coarse inclusions can serve as sources of crack initiation in the BCC-matrix.The synthesized CrMoNbWV HEA exhibited high corrosion resistance, hardness, and wear resistance. A promising way to use the CrMoNbWV HEA

papers.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiMoTi-based HEA coatings with varied B content (x = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5) on Q235 steel
papers.approach: Laser cladding with boron microalloying; microstructural characterization (SEM, EDS), tribological and electrochemical tests
papers.findings: Addition of a small amount of B (x = 0.5) improved the stability of the passive film and reduced corrosion current, while an optimal B content (x = 1) refined the BCC phase and promoted in situ TiB2 formation, leading to improved hardness and dominant abrasive/oxidative wear mechanisms. Excess B led to large TiB2 particles and defects in the passive film.
papers.mechanism: Boron addition triggers secondary TiB2 formation and lattice distortion, which refines the microstructure and enhances both the mechanical barrier (via increased hardness and refined phases) and the formation/stability of a passive oxide film.

papers.title: Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi processed by laser-based consolidation additive manufacturing
papers.approach: Wear testing in ultra-high vacuum to eliminate oxidation; STEM grain size analysis; application of a dynamic amorphization model
papers.findings: The alloy exhibited inverse Hall-Petch behavior with low friction (≈0.3) and extremely low wear rates (≈10⁻⁶ mm³/N-m) in inert environments. Shear induces the formation of a highly refined, near-amorphous surface film which governs friction behavior.
papers.mechanism: Dynamic shear-induced amorphization leads to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline (or near-amorphous) layer that reduces grain size and alters shear strength, providing an improved mechanical barrier against wear.

papers.title: Erosion and Corrosion Resistance Performance of Laser Metal Deposited High-Entropy Alloy Coatings at Hellisheidi Geothermal Site.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMo0.85 and Al0.5CoCrFeNi HEA coatings on carbon and stainless steels
papers.approach: Laser metal deposition followed by field tests in high-temperature geothermal environments; microstructural and surface analysis via SEM/BSE and profilometry
papers.findings: Both HEA coatings exhibit high corrosion resistance when manufacturing defects are minimized. However, on carbon steel substrates, manufacturing-induced cracks can lead to premature corrosion, whereas deposition on stainless steel yielded excellent performance.
papers.mechanism: The intrinsic wear and corrosion resistance rely on the microstructural quality and the ability to maintain a stable passive film; however, defects introduced during processing (thermal and stress-induced cracks) can override the protective mechanisms.

papers.title: Study on cavitation erosion-corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu₀.₁ high entropy alloy in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMoCu₀.₁ HEA tested in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under cavitation erosion (CE) conditions
papers.approach: Combined cavitation erosion tests with electrochemical noise (EN) analysis; morphological observations and surface roughness measurements
papers.findings: There is a significant synergistic effect where corrosion accelerates the erosion damage. With increased CE time, the passive film degrades and selective phase corrosion diminishes as the FCC phase is removed, altering the distribution of corrosion energies.
papers.mechanism: Corrosion-induced degradation of the passive film—exacerbated under mechanical cavitation—leads to a feedback mechanism in which the mechanical damage continuously impairs the passivation capacity and thus increases overall degradation.

papers.title: Study on Microstructures and Properties of FeCoNiCuAlSiₓ High-Entropy Alloy Composite Coatings by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: FeCoNiCuAlSiₓ HEA composite coatings (x = 0 to 2.0) on 65 Mn substrates
papers.approach: Laser cladding with variable Si content; metallographic microscopy, Vickers hardness testing, friction and wear testing, and electrochemical analysis
papers.findings: Increasing Si content induces a phase transformation from FCC to BCC with a finer dendritic structure, elevating microhardness and decreasing wear rate (up to a 55% decrease) while also improving corrosion potential and lowering current density.
papers.mechanism: Si-induced phase transformation and microstructural refinement jointly enhance wear resistance by increasing hardness and support a more uniform passive film formation that improves corrosion resistance.

papers.title: Effect of Adding Molybdenum on Microstructure, Hardness, and Corrosion Resistance of an AlCoCrFeNiMo₀.₂₅ High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiMo₀.₂₅ HEA produced by arc melting
papers.approach: Comparison with AISI 304L and AlCoCrFeNi without Mo; potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution
papers.findings: Mo addition leads to the formation of secondary phases (σ and minor FCC) that fragment grains into a mosaic structure, thereby increasing hardness and enhancing corrosion resistance compared to the base HEA.
papers.mechanism: Mo triggers microstructural fragmentation and secondary phase formation, which contributes to a dual benefit: higher mechanical strength (thus resisting wear) and improved passivation effectiveness (thus resisting corrosion).

papers.title: Effect of Thermal Shock on Properties of a Strongly Amorphous AlCrTiZrMo High-Entropy Alloy Film.
papers.system: Amorphous AlCrTiZrMo HEA films produced by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition
papers.approach: Annealing at different temperatures (400 °C, 600 °C, 800 °C) with subsequent tribocorrosion performance monitoring (OCP and COF measurements during sliding in 3.5 wt% NaCl)
papers.findings: Annealing at 800 °C for 1 h resulted in formation of a dense ZrTiO₄ composite oxide layer, leading to the highest tribocorrosion resistance, with minimized fluctuations in OCP and friction coefficient and extremely low wear rate.
papers.mechanism: Thermal shock leads to a controlled crystallization/oxidation process that forms a stable, protective oxide layer on the near-surface, combining high hardness with chemical passivation to reduce both wear and corrosion.

papers.title: Refractory CrMoNbWV High-Entropy Alloy Manufactured by Mechanical Alloying and Spark Plasma Sintering: Evolution of Microstructure and Properties.
papers.system: CrMoNbWV HEA produced via mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) at different temperatures
papers.approach: Processing via MA and SPS followed by microstructural (XRD, SEM) analysis, wear tests, and corrosion testing in H₂SO₄ solution
papers.findings: Higher SPS temperatures lead to grain coarsening in the BCC phase and a reduction in Laves phase content, which affects hardness and wear resistance. The alloy exhibits excellent wear and corrosion resistance, with properties comparable to other high-performance HEAs but at lower density.
papers.mechanism: The balance between a fine-grained BCC matrix, protective Laves phases, and the formation of minor oxide inclusions governs the dual resistance to wear (via high hardness) and corrosion (through low passive film degradation).

papers.title: Microstructural, Mechanical, and Electrochemical Characterization of CrMoNbTiZr High-Entropy Alloy for Biomedical Application.
papers.system: CrMoNbTiZr HEA produced by powder mixing and spark plasma sintering
papers.approach: Comprehensive characterization including compression tests, wear testing, Vickers hardness, and electrochemical measurements in PBS and Hanks’ solutions
papers.findings: The alloy, comprising primarily BCC and Laves phases (with reinforcing carbides), shows high hardness, excellent wear resistance, and bio-corrosion rates comparable to cortical bone, making it promising for biomedical applications.
papers.mechanism: The synergy of a dual-phase structure (a softer BCC phase offering ductility and a harder Laves phase providing wear resistance) along with in situ carbide formation yields a protective mechanical and electrochemical barrier.

papers.title: Microstructure and Properties of AlₓCr₁₋ₓCoFeNi High-Entropy Alloys Prepared by Spark Plasma Sintering.
papers.system: AlₓCr₁₋ₓCoFeNi HEAs with varying Al content prepared by SPS
papers.approach: Spark plasma sintering with systematic variation of Al content; friction, wear, and corrosion tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution
papers.findings: Increasing Al content promotes phase transformation from FCC to BCC, enhances hardness and friction behavior, and influences selective corrosion due to the coexistence of Cr-rich and Cr-poor phases. An optimum composition (e.g., Al₀.₅Cr₀.₅CoFeNi) shows the best combined mechanical and corrosion performance.
papers.mechanism: The induced phase transformation improves mechanical resistance while reducing the fraction of phases that are prone to localized corrosion, thereby balancing the competing demands of wear and corrosion resistance.

established: Microstructural refinement (whether via alloying additions like B, Si, Mo or processing routes like SPS and laser cladding) is correlated with improved wear resistance.
The formation and stability of a passive oxide or amorphous near-surface layer are critical for corrosion resistance in HEAs.
Defect-free and single-phase or uniformly refined microstructures tend to resist synergistic degradation better than multi-phase or defect-prone coatings.

approaches_tried.approach: Alloying additions (B, Si, Mo, Cu) to modify phase composition and refine microstructure
approaches_tried.outcome: Significant improvements in hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion behavior when optimized; however, excessive addition can introduce defects or secondary phases that harm passivation

approaches_tried.approach: Processing modifications such as laser cladding, mechanical alloying with SPS, and vacuum arc melting
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced densification and microstructural control leading to improved combined wear and corrosion resistance; results are highly sensitive to process-induced defects and thermal histories

approaches_tried.approach: Environmental control (e.g., UHV conditions to suppress oxidation)
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed mechanisms like dynamic amorphization which lower friction and wear rates, though not directly translatable to harsh corrosive environments

mechanisms: Dynamic formation of a protective, ultra-fine (amorphous or nanocrystalline) surface layer under mechanical shear
Formation of stable passive oxide films (e.g., ZrTiO₄) that self-heal during wear
Microstructural refinement resulting in barrier effects at grain and phase boundaries that resist both plastic deformation and corrosive attack
disagreements: Whether multi-phase alloys with selective phase corrosion (e.g., Cr-rich vs. Cr-poor) offer superior long-term resistance compared to single-phase, uniformly refined structures

The role of secondary precipitates: some studies attribute improvement to their formation, while others note that excessive or coarse precipitates may undermine passive film stability and overall durability
open_questions: Can a single mechanistic framework based on the dynamic formation of a protective near-surface layer robustly explain both wear and corrosion resistance across diverse HEA compositions and processing routes?
How do various processing-induced defects interact with in situ film formation under simultaneous wear and corrosion conditions?
What are the limits of passivation when the dynamic mechanical damage continuously alters the microstructure?
opportunities: Conduct a controlled comparison between HEA samples with nearly identical bulk chemistry and hardness but different surface states (e.g., pre-induced nanocrystalline/amorphous layers versus conventional surfaces) under identical wear-corrosion testing conditions
Combine in situ tribocorrosion measurements with real-time surface characterization to map the evolution of the protective layer during mechanical loading
Explore subtle variations in alloying (e.g., fine-tuning B or Si levels) to identify the threshold at which passivation and microstructural refinement optimally synergize
Test the hypothesis across environments ranging from inert (UHV) to highly oxidative (NaCl or geothermal conditions) to define the regime where the protective mechanism holds or fails

An observation that would falsify the hypothesis is if intentionally generating a dynamic near-surface protective layer (via pre-treatment or controlled deformation) does not lead to improvements in both wear and corrosion resistance compared to a matched baseline

directions.direction: Alloying modifications to induce secondary precipitates that refine microstructure and indirectly stabilize the passive film (e.g., boron addition leading to TiB2 formation).
directions.assessment: Addresses both wear and corrosion by mechanically strengthening the surface (through microstructural refinement) and chemically stabilizing passivation. Supported by evidence in PMC12565319 and PMC12525669; constraints are respected and the study is feasible via laser cladding.

directions.direction: Utilizing processing-induced dynamic surface modifications where shear (under wear) induces an ultra-nanocrystalline or near-amorphous surface layer that provides a self-replenishing protective barrier.
directions.assessment: Directly tests the mechanism of dynamic film formation under mechanical loading. Inert environment studies (PMC7311485) support the concept, although extension to corrosive environments adds complexity. Feasible with in situ tribocorrosion measurements.

directions.direction: Applying thermal shock or controlled annealing to trigger the in situ formation of a dense, protective composite oxide layer on the HEA surface.
directions.assessment: Directly attacks dual degradation by creating a stable, passivating oxide film that resists both wear and corrosion. Prior evidence (PMC10456374) supports benefits in tribocorrosion resistance. Conditions (e.g., 800 °C/1 h) are well established and falsifiable by mechanical removal of the oxide layer.

directions.direction: Tailoring microstructure via processing conditions (e.g., spark plasma sintering) to produce fine-grained matrices with controlled secondary phases that offer simultaneous mechanical and chemical protection.
directions.assessment: Controls grain size and secondary phase distribution (such as Laves phases) to moderate deformation and passivation. Evidence from refractory HEAs (PMC7866258) shows correlations with improved wear and corrosion resistance. Feasible via controlled sintering temperature studies.
